Over the past two years, AI recording hardware has become one of the hottest areas for startups. From rings and pendants to clip-on earphones and wristbands, more and more products are using "recording" as an entry point, branching into two distinct paths: one category positions itself as productivity tools, focusing on scenarios such as document generation, meeting minutes, and knowledge organization—users turn them on when needed and off when done. The other category targets always-on scenarios, aiming to continuously record users' offline voice, conversations, and experiences, transforming them into long-term context for AI. The latter targets a massive user base: 80 to 100 million small and medium-sized business owners worldwide. Compared to average consumers, this group makes numerous decisions daily but rarely has a personal assistant. Many critical conversations happen outside the computer screen: in coffee shops, on the road, in hallways, or even during impromptu meetings. These pieces of information, which are hard to capture systematically, directly influence their judgment. This makes them among the earliest adopters of AI, yet they also feel the limitations first: large models seem to know almost everything, but they lack the ability to continuously understand a single individual, forcing users to re-enter tedious background information with every query. excerpt_i18n.en: In 2026, the Ministry of Education and four other departments issued the "AI + Education" Action Plan, which explicitly requires a tiered enhancement of teachers' AI digital literacy and the comprehensive construction of a new human-machine collaborative classroom model. The policy direction is clear, but discussions on implementation are still ongoing. On July 23, Zhou Lei, Vice President of Fudan University, stated in an exclusive interview with People's Daily Online: "Amid the wave of intelligent transformation, teaching innovation is more closely tied to the essence of education than ever before." He also pointed out that the primary capability upgrade for frontline teachers is shifting from "AI tool users" to "intelligent instructional designers." This statement precisely captures the deep anxiety shared by many schools—AI applications in education are not scarce, but most remain superficial, struggling to truly serve individualized teaching, and the transformation of teachers lacks a complete support system. Currently, there are three structural challenges in AI-empowered education: First, the structural shortage of teachers is difficult to resolve. County and rural schools suffer from a scarcity of key teachers, and under large class sizes, teachers cannot simultaneously address underperforming students and challenge advanced ones, spending excessive time on standardized tasks like academic statistics and exercise organization, leaving no room for value guidance, emotional nurturing, and other irreplaceable educational work. Second, the superficiality of AI applications is hard to overcome. Fragmented smart products on the market can only push content, unable to simulate students' true thinking gaps. Teachers lack a complete theoretical framework to support personalized instructional design, making it difficult to transform into classroom "directors" and learning designers. Third, the AI transformation of teachers lacks a supporting system. Schools purchase tools sporadically and explore integration paths on their own.
